title: Dyer v. MacDougall (1952)
summary: The plaintiff’s hope of discrediting denying witnesses did not supply the missing affirmative proof of slander.
notes: This short note should be compared with Adickes, where circumstantial events and a material gap in the moving evidence supplied more than a bare hope of disbelief.

sections.Parties: Dyer sued for slander; the persons who allegedly made or heard the statements denied the allegations.
sections.Material Facts: All persons present at the alleged occasion supplied affidavits denying the slanderous statements. The plaintiff relied on the possibility that their appearance and demeanor at trial would lead a jury to reject their denials and infer that the statements had been made.
sections.Procedural History: The district court granted summary judgment. The Second Circuit affirmed.
sections.Issue: Could the prospect of disbelief based on witness demeanor alone create enough evidence for a trial?
sections.Holding: No on this record. It did not supply an adequate basis for a sustainable verdict establishing the affirmative claim.
sections.Reasoning: The court distinguished disbelieving a denial from having sufficient affirmative evidence that the alleged statement occurred. It also discussed the inability of an appellate court to review vanished demeanor evidence as the sole support for such a result. The decision illustrates the production burden that remains even where witness credibility could theoretically be challenged.

learning.why: The plaintiff’s hope of discrediting denying witnesses did not supply the missing affirmative proof of slander.

topics.cp-inferences: A hope that a jury would disbelieve all witnesses did not itself provide affirmative evidence of the plaintiff’s claim.
topics.cp-burden-production: The plaintiff still needed a basis on which a reasonable verdict in his favor could rest.

mnemonic.rationale: A slander no witness would admit
